SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

An enemy sows counterfeit grain among the good seed by night.
Where does the Old Testament teach two seeds in one field?
In its third chapter, in the sentence passed on the serpent:

And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.

Two seeds, two families, growing in the same world since Eden.
Job knew the picture of weeds where grain was sown — “Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley” (Job 31:40) — and Isaiah's vineyard, planted entirely with “the choicest vine,” nonetheless “brought forth wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2).

The harvest the disciples’ Scriptures already knew as the day of reckoning: “Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13); “O Judah, he hath set an harvest for thee” (Hosea 6:11); Babylon herself is a threshingfloor whose “time of her harvest shall come” (Jeremiah 51:33).
And the fire at the end was Malachi's closing word:

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

On that day one shall again “discern between the righteous and the wicked” (Malachi 3:18), the ungodly driven “like the chaff” (Psalm 1:4).
Write the derivation out: an enemy's seed grows beside God's seed in one field, indistinguishable until fruit, and a harvest-day of burning sorts them.

The Teacher's key: the field is the world; the good seed, the children of the kingdom; the tares, “the children of the wicked one”; the enemy, the devil — the serpent whose seed Genesis 3:15 named; the harvest, “the end of the world” — the age; the tares bound in bundles “to burn them” (Matthew 13:30, 38-40).
Item for item, the derivation stands.
Two parables, two perfect scores — for a reader who had done the assigned reading.

The kingdom enters the world as the least of seeds:

The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.

Derive it.
The seed-to-tree movement begins with one life and ends with a people.
Isaiah says it plainly of Abraham: “I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him” (Isaiah 51:2).
The disciple's Scriptures also define the least as the chosen beginning: “The LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people” (Deuteronomy 7:7) — a verse the remnant chapter will weigh again.
One man became Israel; the least planting became a nation.
And the disciples had already watched God plant one tender life and grow it into the shelter of the world, in a parable He decoded Himself:

I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain… and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell.

God spoke that as a riddle to be decoded (Ezekiel 17:2, 12) and closed it with the rule the mustard seed obeys: “I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree” (Ezekiel 17:24).
Daniel grades the same picture for a king: the great tree in whose boughs “the fowls of the heaven dwelt” is a kingdom in its head — “It is thou, O king” (Daniel 4:12, 22).
So a tree grows from one planted person into a house, people, or nation; the smallest planting becomes the greatest shelter, and the birds of every wing are the peoples nesting in its reach — the stone that became “a great mountain, and filled the whole earth” (Daniel 2:35), told in a gardener's vocabulary; the mountain has a case study of its own in Part Six.

Even the strange word “lodge” was derivable.
Ezekiel's “dwell” is shakan, the tabernacle word, and Matthew's Greek keeps it — kataskēnoō, to pitch one's tent — and the prophets had promised the nations exactly that tent-rest in a Person: “a Branch shall grow out of his roots… and in that day there shall be a root of Jesse… to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11:1, 10); “Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH” (Zechariah 6:12).
The birds lodge in the branches because the nations find rest in the Branch.

This parable Jesus left unkeyed — He supplied no decoding, and He did not need to, for God had already published His own in Ezekiel.
But carry the first parable's edge with you: fowls also devour seed, and Assyria's sheltering cedar housed “all great nations” on its way to the axe (Ezekiel 31:6) — the branches that shelter the nations shelter what the nations bring.

Next comes the strangest of the seven, if the symbols mean what Scripture made them mean:

The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.

Derive it from Torah, where every hearer of Moses began.
Leaven is purged from every house before the feast (Exodus 12:15); it is banned from the altar absolutely — “ye shall burn no leaven… in any offering of the LORD made by fire” (Leviticus 2:11); Amos names a leavened offering in sarcasm to a rebellious people — “offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with leaven… for this liketh you” (Amos 4:5); and Hosea watches adulterous Ephraim rise like dough, the baker idle “until it be leavened” (Hosea 7:4).
Not once in Moses or the prophets is leaven a figure of anything good: it is corruption working hidden through the whole lump.

Tradition reads this parable as the gospel quietly permeating the world — but the derived vocabulary refuses, and the Teacher's own usage grades the tradition down: leaven is “the doctrine of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16:12), and Paul cries “purge out the old leaven” (1 Corinthians 5:7).
If the symbol holds, the parable is a warning laid alongside the tares: as the enemy sows counterfeit wheat in the field, so corrupt teaching, hidden in the meal by stealth, works “till the whole was leavened.”

The parable flags two words this book has not yet mapped: the woman who hides it, and the three measures of meal — the very quantity Sarah kneaded for the LORD at Mamre (Genesis 18:6).
These candidates receive the same test as every other: gather the uses, and let Scripture define them.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.

The field we may carry forward from the tares — the exam allows a student to reuse a graded answer: the field is the world.
And the treasure has a definition older than the parable, spoken at Sinai to the whole nation:

…if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people…

“The LORD hath chosen Jacob unto himself, and Israel for his peculiar treasure” (Psalm 135:4).
And this treasure is hidden — Asaph says so of the saints themselves: the enemy takes “crafty counsel against thy people,” consulting “against thy hidden ones” (Psalm 83:3).
The treasure hid in the field is the covenant people hidden in the world, the remnant scattered and unseen — and the man who sells all he has to buy the whole field for the treasure's sake is the Redeemer.

Grade the common teaching against that, for this parable is almost always preached inverted: God — or salvation — is the treasure, and we are the fortunate finder who gladly gives up everything.
Test it: the buyer “selleth all that he hath” — and in this same gospel, the one man told to do exactly that “went away sorrowful” (Matthew 19:21-22).
Disciples do forsake all — Peter says so five verses later and is not corrected (Matthew 19:27), and “whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33) — but no disciple ever did one thing: buy the field.
The field is the world by the Teacher's own key, and the buyer purchases all of it to possess the treasure — a price One alone paid: “though he was rich… he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), “the propitiation… for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2) — and the treasure was defined at Sinai before the parable ever borrowed it: the people are the treasure, and the seeker is God.

The Hebrew Matthew tradition sharpens the picture, reading gold hidden in the field — and no man buys a field for gold coins; coins you pocket and walk away.
Gold in a field is ore: scattered through the ground, dug, crushed, and refined — exactly what the prophets say the Owner does with His treasure: “I will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried” (Zechariah 13:9); “when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold” (Job 23:10).
He buys the whole field, mines His people out of it, and refines what He mines.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.

This one the Teacher left unkeyed, and this book will give it a chapter of its own; here, set down the floor the disciples’ own Scriptures supply.
The derivation stands on the Old Testament the disciples held. The Hebrew peninim is by Strong's own definition “probably a pearl (as round)”. [Footnote: The KJV renders peninim as “rubies.” The full lexical case is documented at TimeTested.Bible under “Peninim: Why Pearl Fits Better Than Ruby.”] Wisdom is “more precious than pearls” (Proverbs 3:15), her price “above pearls” (Job 28:18), and the virtuous woman — the bride of a later chapter — is “far above pearls” (Proverbs 31:10). The seeker who “searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Proverbs 2:4) is the merchant himself, one figure in Solomon's book.

A pearl is drawn up out of the sea — the nations, as the net will show in a moment — formed slowly, in secret, around a wound; and the merchant seeking many goodly pearls finds one of great price and sells everything, for the kingdom is not a collection; it is one bride, bought whole.
And the Pearl chapter will carry the derivation a ring deeper, for the parable holds more than a jewel: the gates of the city John saw are waiting inside it, and Scripture keeps its one pearl of great price where no tradition has thought to look for it.

The Teacher gave no key here; He speaks to hearers expected to understand “a proverb, and the interpretation” (Proverbs 1:5-6) from the Scriptures they already hold.
Test all things against that word, and “hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21, NKJV).

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.

Derive it — the fishermen in the boat needed no help at all.
The sea is the peoples, and Habakkuk had already put men in it:

And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?
They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad.

The fishers are sent by God Himself: “Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the LORD, and they shall fish them” (Jeremiah 16:16).
The catch “of every kind” is Ezekiel's river-vision, where the healed waters swarm and “the fishers shall stand… their fish shall be according to their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many” (Ezekiel 47:10).
And the sorting on the shore was Torah before it was parable — fins and scales, clean from unclean (Leviticus 11:9-10): these men were fishermen of Israel; they had sorted every catch of their lives by Leviticus.

The Teacher's key: “So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just” (Matthew 13:49) — the same verdict the harvest told in field-language: wheat to the barn and tares to the fire, good fish to vessels and bad away.
Two landscapes, one message — the sown field and the peopled sea — because the kingdom is drawing from both.

Notice where He sits as He says it.
Matthew staged the discourse before writing a word of it: Jesus “went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore” (Matthew 13:2) — the Teacher seated in a vessel upon the sea He has just decoded, casting the word like the net into the peoples at its edge.
The sermon acts out its own vocabulary while it is spoken — the prophets' habit the Signs and Similitudes chapter takes up next — and what the vessel He sits in means, The Ship, ch. 41 proves in full.

Jesus then did what He had been saying.
With the symbols in hand, the feeding of the multitude reads as the lived parable it is — John even calls it a sign (John 6:14).
A boy has “five barley loaves, and two small fishes” (John 6:9); from them a multitude is fed, and “they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full” (Matthew 14:20).

Five loaves: the five books of the Law, the bread of the word — and barley, the humble firstfruits grain Scripture itself pins to Israel: when the barley loaf tumbled into Midian’s camp, the watchman decoded it inside the dream — “this is nothing else save the sword of Gideon… a man of Israel” (Judges 7:13-14).
Two fishes: witnesses — for the Law itself fixed the number, “at the mouth of two witnesses… shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15), and the Lord sent His fishers of men out “by two and two” (Mark 6:7).
The bread is blessed, broken, and handed to the disciples, and the disciples to the people — and as the word is shared it multiplies, until the hungry are filled and twelve baskets remain, one for each tribe.
The Law, carried by witnesses, feeds the famished, and there is more left at the end than was held at the start.

The crowd that watched it graded the sign correctly: “This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world” (John 6:14) — they read a similitude and recognized the Prophet like unto Moses, who had also fed a multitude on bread from heaven.

The scene has a second act, and it grades the hearers.
The next day the same crowd hunts Him down, and He tells them what they missed: “Ye seek me, not because ye saw the signs, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled” (John 6:26) — they had eaten the sign without reading it.
So He states the similitude at full strength — my flesh is meat indeed — and the room divides: many go back at the hard saying, milk-hearers meeting strong meat (John 6:55, 60, 66).
Peter passes, holding the key Jesus handed out before they went: the flesh profits nothing, the words are spirit and life (John 6:63, 68). [Footnote: The scene that opened this book; the Introduction walks the exchange word by word.]
The saying sorted the hearers, exactly as Isaiah said the concealed word would; they left because they did not know His symbolic language.

Tally the exam.
Where the Teacher supplied an answer key — the sower, the tares, the net — every key matched what the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had already put in the disciples’ hands: Isaiah's seed, Jeremiah's fallow heart, Abram's fowls, Hosea's thorn-grown altars, the two seeds of Eden, Joel's sickle, Malachi's stubble, Leviticus’ sorted catch.
That is why the score was owed: not one answer hung on a single verse.
Seed, ground, fowls, thorns — each stands on a pattern laid across Moses and the prophets, witness upon witness; the accountability was proportioned to how established the pattern was.

Where He supplied none — the mustard tree, the leaven, the treasure, the pearl — the same Scriptures carry the reader most of the way, and mark plainly where the derivation ends and the testing begins.
That is why His rebuke was fair, and why His question was not rhetorical.
The disciples answered it — “Yea, Lord” (Matthew 13:51) — and He immediately described what such a reader becomes:

Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.

Things new and old — the old is the derivation, and the new is its fulfillment; the dark sayings “of old… which our fathers have told us,” and the kingdom now speaking them fluently.
That is the reader this book aims to form: not a keeper of its conclusions but a scribe instructed — one who can take a text he has never been taught, derive it from what Scripture itself defined, mark honestly what remains under test, and go gather the uses.

Before leaving the exam, count what it cost.
The seven parables, with the householder's saying that seals them, run twenty-six verses — some five hundred and eighty-five words — and carry more than fifty decodable terms, one symbolic use every five words, defined by more than eighty passages from twenty-three books of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
A few minutes in a boat, and the sermon is three times larger than itself — nearly every phrase leaning on text written centuries before.

Books were costly then; copying was slow; memory was the library; a text composed under that economy wastes nothing.
So stands the question the rest of this book will test: what if all Scripture is this dense?

Everything that follows in this book stands or falls with the method you have just watched graded; once the method holds, the conclusions are arithmetic.
The language does not stop, and neither does the exam.
“Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.”

The four winds are held back “till we have sealed the servants of our God,” under the command “Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees” (Revelation 7:3).
The sea is the restless mass of peoples; the tree stands beside it in that verse, and Scripture defines it just as plainly.
When Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree filling the earth, Daniel does not guess; he decodes it:

It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth.

The tree is the king together with his dominion — Babylon embodied in its covenant head as a living, rooted body.
The scale follows the tree's growth: it begins as one planted life, grows into a house or lineage, and may mature into a people or nation.
The person is not an exception to the national symbol; the person is its seed and covenant head.
The same equation recurs across the prophets — Israel is a “vine” (Hosea 10:1), Assyria a “cedar” (Ezekiel 31:3), the covenant people an “olive tree” (Romans 11).
Whatever the scale, the tree is a rooted life known by what grows from it — and the species itself helps identify its character.

The whole sequence is written in the history of Abraham: “I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him” (Isaiah 51:2).
One man becomes a house, tribes, and a nation.
Ezekiel plants one “tender” twig from David's royal cedar and watches it become “a goodly cedar” under whose branches birds of every wing dwell (Ezekiel 17:22-23).
Jesus gathers the same movement into the mustard seed: one seed is sown, “but when it is grown… becometh a tree,” and the birds lodge in its branches (Matthew 13:31-32).
Seed, person, house, nation: one continuous growth.

The kind of tree is no accident; in the prophetic histories it often names the nation or house.
Israel appears as the trees of the covenant land — the vine (Psalm 80:8), the fig, and the olive: “The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree” (Jeremiah 11:16); often all at once — “I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree” (Hosea 9:10), and “he hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree” (Joel 1:7).
The gentile empires are the towering forest trees — Assyria a cedar, and Pharaoh likened to the same “among the trees of Eden” (Ezekiel 31:3, 18).

When Jesus curses a fig tree (Matthew 21:19), or tells of a barren one in a vineyard (Luke 13:6), He is not teaching horticulture; He is pronouncing on Israel.
The kind of tree identifies the rooted body — and often its character: the cedar’s imperial height, the vine’s call to fruit, the fig’s covenant standing.

The tree is a precise symbol because its parts carry meaning.
Paul lays out the anatomy with the olive tree:

And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree…

The root is the body's origin and covenant foundation — the patriarch or Head from whom the life proceeds, and the covenant word that makes the whole holy.
The branches are the members who grow from or are joined to it.
Branches can be broken off (cut from the nation) and others grafted in, and the tree persists through the exchange.
A house or nation is a living structure: rooted in its origin, composed of members, able to lose some and gain others without ceasing to be itself.

A tree is judged by what it produces.
Jesus states it as a rule:

…every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit.

Whether the tree is a man, a house, or a nation, its fruit is what it produces; this is how a living body is weighed — by what it does.
The barren tree is cut down:

Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

This is the standard image for judgment upon a rooted life, individual or corporate.
The axe “is laid unto the root of the trees” (Luke 3:9); Babylon’s great tree is felled — “Hew the tree down” (Daniel 4:23, though a stump is left for regrowth).
And a nation can be fruitful in form yet condemned: Israel was “an empty vine” that “bringeth forth fruit unto himself” (Hosea 10:1) — full of works, empty of covenant purpose.

When Scripture sets the figure at national scale, the world’s nations together make a forest, and Scripture treats them so.
The tree-texts that decoded the mustard seed — Ezekiel’s riddle of the low tree exalted and Daniel’s great tree that was a king — are the forest’s charter (Ezekiel 17; Daniel 4) [Footnote: They decoded the mustard seed in the chapter The Parables of the Kingdom.], and the riddle’s closing word surveys the whole stand:

And all the trees of the field shall know that I the LORD have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish…

Here “all the trees of the field” are all the nations; God deals with them as a gardener deals with trees — felling the proud, raising the low.

The same parable fixes what the cedar is — and is not: the “high cedar” of that chapter is the royal house of David itself, and God promises to crop “of the highest branch” a tender twig and plant it “in the mountain of the height of Israel,” where it becomes “a goodly cedar” sheltering “all fowl of every wing” (Ezekiel 17:22-23).
Assyria a cedar, David's house a cedar, the righteous growing “like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12): the cedar is height and majesty, whoever bears it — the symbol is the stature, not a badge of the heathen.
And the great trees shelter others: under Nebuchadnezzar’s tree “the beasts of the field had shadow… and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs” (Daniel 4:12) — the peoples and tribes that live within an empire’s reach.

This fixes the tree among the symbols already defined.
A mountain is a kingdom — the seat of ruling authority.
A tree at this scale is the nation, the living body of a people, which grows on the mountain, under its jurisdiction.
The sea is those same peoples in their unrooted, turbulent state — beasts rise from the sea (Daniel 7), but shelter under the tree (Daniel 4).
And beneath the tree is the grass — the individual mortal, which is its own study.
Kingdom, rooted people, mortal flesh: mountain, tree, grass.

Two more branches of the symbol remain before the beasts.
The pair of olive trees Zechariah saw return in Revelation as the two witnesses — covenant trees standing before God (Zechariah 4:14; Revelation 11:4), taken up in the Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim chapter.
The symbol's beginning is the righteous man: “he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season” (Psalm 1:3); the redeemed are “trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD” (Isaiah 61:3).
Jesus makes the personal scale explicit: “a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit” becomes, four verses later, “a good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good” (Luke 6:43-45).
As that fruit becomes seed in others, the man stands as the root or head of a multigenerational house, as Abraham grows into Israel, Nebuchadnezzar embodies his kingdom, and the cedar in Ezekiel 17 embodies David's royal house.
Grass is the mortal in his frailty; the tree is a life rooted in covenant, watered, branching beyond itself, and bearing fruit.

Look again at the beasts that sheltered under Nebuchadnezzar's tree (Daniel 4:12) — all the animals under its branches.
For the beast is the other figure of a nation.
Where the tree is a people rooted and fruitful, the beast is a people wild and ravening; and Daniel decodes it as plainly as he did the tree:

These great beasts, which are four, are four kings, which shall arise out of the earth.

A beast is a kingdom, and the kind of beast marks which — as the species of tree marked which nation.
The lion, the bear, the leopard, and the nameless fourth are four empires (Daniel 7); “the ram… are the kings of Media and Persia… the rough goat is the king of Grecia” (Daniel 8:20-21).
And these come up not from the garden but “from the sea” (Daniel 7:3) — the same peoples, seen now as predators rising from the restless deep.

The two figures meet in one man.
The king who was the great tree is sentenced to become a beast — “Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him” (Daniel 4:16) — until he “did eat grass as oxen” (Daniel 4:33).
The ruler who forgets God is carried down through the whole order, from the tree that filled the earth to a beast on all fours feeding on grass; for “man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish” (Psalm 49:20).

This is why clean and unclean divide the animals as the covenant divides mankind.
God's own are the flock — the sheep who hear His voice; the nations are the wild beasts.
So when God opens the door to the Gentiles He shows Peter a sheet of “all manner of fourfooted beasts… and wild beasts, and creeping things” (Acts 10:12), with the command “Rise, Peter; kill, and eat… What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:13-15).
To kill and to eat is the language of covenant-making — the sacrifice slain and the meal shared that seal it — so the vision is God taking the nations into covenant.
Peter gives its meaning himself, twice over (Acts 10:28; 11:4-18):

Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.

The unclean animals are the nations, cleansed by covenant.

It is why the Gentile is called a dog — “It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it to dogs,” and the woman answers, “yet the dogs eat of the crumbs” (Matthew 15:26-27): outside the house, an unclean animal, until she is brought in.
Mark keeps the table in her answer — “the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs” (Mark 7:28) — and the table is the dog's defining line: the unclean beast outside the covenant meal.
And the crucifixion psalm shows that beast at its work: “Dogs have compassed me… they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 22:16) — the psalm rings the cross with beasts, the bulls of Bashan, the roaring lion, the dogs — and it was the dog, the Gentile power of Rome, whose hands drove the nails.

At the national scale, tree or beast, forest or field, clean or unclean, the figures concern the peoples of the earth, which God plants and fells, tames and cleanses.

Where the trees are nations, a garden — a planted stand of trees — is a grouping of nations.
Ezekiel says as much: he sets Egypt among “the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God” (Ezekiel 31:9), and names them — “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude” (Ezekiel 31:18).
The garden of God is a field of nation-trees.

Read so, a recurring charge in Isaiah changes register.
Isaiah indicts Judah for worship “in gardens” — “that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick” (Isaiah 65:3), and shames her “for the gardens that ye have chosen” (Isaiah 1:29).
The usual reading makes these literal pagan groves; by the symbol they are the nations Judah chose to run to — sacrificing among them, trusting in them — and the sentence fits the crime: “ye shall be as an oak whose leaf fadeth, and as a garden that hath no water” (Isaiah 1:30).
She chose the gardens of the nations; she becomes a dead garden herself.

Which unlocks the hardest of them:

They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together…

By the symbol it is plain: they sanctify themselves in the gardens — among the nations; behind one — following after one of them; eating the swine, the abomination, and the mouse — taking up the nations’ unclean ways.
They enter the nations, follow one, eat its abominations, and share its end — “consumed together.”

The traditional reading takes this as a literal garden-cult, but it rests on a word that is not in the text.
The Hebrew says only “after one in the midst”; “tree” is supplied by the translators — and with it gone, the literal reading has nothing left to name, so it guesses: a sacred tree, a priest in the midst, a deity called “One.”
The symbol supplies nothing — “in the gardens, after one” is among the nations, following one — and it reads with the context, for the next verses show the LORD gathering “all nations and tongues” and sending the escaped “unto the nations” (Isaiah 66:18-19).
The whole passage is about the nations; so is the garden.

The end-times setting proves the diet itself eternal.
This is the last judgment — the LORD coming “with fire” to “plead with all flesh” (Isaiah 66:15-16), with all nations gathered to it (Isaiah 66:18).
At that consummation God still consumes those who eat “swine’s flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse.”
The line between clean and unclean is not abolished; it holds to the end of the age.

We have already seen that the law was not abolished but filled full, and that the covenant-name is everlasting — and the food law is part of that law; here it stands as the very ground of the verdict.
Nor does the symbol soften the letter; the two are one act.
To eat the nations’ unclean food is to sit at the nations’ table and take their defilement into yourself — so those who go in among the nations, follow one, and eat as it eats are consumed with it.
The name is eternal, the law is eternal, and the diet is eternal with them.

Return, then, to the sealing.
Before the four winds are loosed, the order is “Hurt not the earth, neither the sea, nor the trees” (Revelation 7:3) — and in that company the trees are rooted peoples, as the sea beside them is the unrooted multitude.
The God who plants and fells the trees of the field is the One the winds obey.

At the political scale, a mountain is a kingdom and a tree is a rooted people; beneath them both stands the shortest-lived figure:

…All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field… The grass withereth, the flower fadeth… but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

Grass is a man — a single mortal, up in the morning and gone by evening. “As for man, his days are as grass… the wind passeth over it, and it is gone” (Psalm 103:15-16); “in the morning it flourisheth… in the evening it is cut down, and withereth” (Psalm 90:5-6).
So the three figures of a people are complete at that scale: a mountain is the kingdom, a tree the rooted people, and the grass the mortal flesh that springs up and dies within it.
The categories describe different aspects, not three mutually exclusive objects: Psalm 1 can call the same man a tree when he is rooted, watered, and fruitful.
The New Testament simply hands the definition back: “all flesh is as grass… The grass withereth” (1 Peter 1:24).

Grass is not only the picture of frailty; it is also the field God farms.
The grains that feed the world — barley and wheat — are grasses, and with them the symbol turns from the withering blade to the standing crop.

The field is sown, and Jesus names both the seed and the soil: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11), scattered on the hearts of men — some hard, some shallow, some good ground that bears.
The seed must die to live:

Except a grain of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.

The word buried in a man is a seed that dies and rises into a harvest.

Grain is grown to be reaped, and the reaping is judgment.
The prophets fixed that meaning long before the parables — Joel's sickle thrust in because the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13); the nations gathered “as the sheaves into the floor” to be threshed by Zion (Micah 4:12-13).
So when Jesus says the same, He is not inventing an image but citing one:

…the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.

The field is the world, the crop is mankind, and the harvest is the day it is cut down.
Revelation reaps the same field with the same words — “Thrust in thy sickle, and reap… for the harvest of the earth is ripe” (Revelation 14:15) — Joel’s command reissued at the end: one chain from the Prophets through the Gospels to the last book.
The harvest has a present tense too: “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (John 4:35); “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Matthew 9:37).

Two different partings happen at the harvest, and the whole vocabulary is Old Testament.
The first is the grain parted from its own husk.
When the threshed wheat is thrown up into the wind, the light, empty chaff is carried off while the heavy grain falls back to the floor — and this is what the wicked are likened to, weightless and rootless: the chaff which the wind drives away (Psalm 1:4), “chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind” (Isaiah 17:13) — the very kingdoms of the Mountain chapter, blown off like husks.
John the Baptist says it in one breath and expects to be understood: “he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12).

The second parting is between two different plants.
The tares are not the wheat's own husk but a weed sown among it — darnel, which mimics the wheat so closely that the two cannot be told apart until the ear forms.
That is the enemy's work, and the Teacher's key has already graded it: the field is the world, the good seed are the children of the kingdom, and the tares are the children of the wicked one (Matthew 13:38). [Footnote: Derived and graded in the chapter The Parables of the Kingdom.]

The two are gathered by different means to one end.
The chaff is winnowed off by the wind; the tares are bound in bundles for the fire while the wheat alone is gathered into the barn (Matthew 13:30) — the counterfeit gathered with the counterfeit, the grain kept.
The threshingfloor is the day of judgment, and it misses nothing: neither the empty husk nor the planted lie.

Even the sifting carries mercy:

I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as grain is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth.

It is the promise the Lord repeated to Peter under the same figure — sifted as wheat, but prayed for, and kept (Luke 22:31-32).
The shaking is real; the grain is not lost.

One grain is reaped before all the rest.
Barley ripens first, in the spring, and the law commanded that its first sheaf be brought and waved before the LORD — “a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest” (Leviticus 23:10) — the pledge of the whole harvest to come.
That sheaf is Christ: “now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept” (1 Corinthians 15:20), raised in the very season of the wave sheaf, the first of a harvest that rises after Him.

Barley is the humble, early grain — the loaf that is Israel tumbling into Midian's camp, the five loaves from which a multitude is fed (Judges 7:13; John 6:9).
The firstfruits are few and lowly, but they carry the whole field in promise.

Grain ground and baked becomes bread, and “man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3) — the bread is the word.

What, then, is leaven?
It is bread soured.
The very consonants that spell it also spell vinegar, an embittered heart, a cruel man; leaven is the loaf turned impure — fermented, puffed up, gone off.
Leaven is corrupt doctrine working through the whole lump — purged from every house before Passover, banned from every offering on the altar (Exodus 12:15; Leviticus 2:11; Matthew 16:12; 1 Corinthians 5:6-7). [Footnote: Derived in the chapter The Parables of the Kingdom.]
So the bread offered to God is unleavened — the feast kept “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8) — a pure and unsoured word.

Set it together and the parables come clear.
When Jesus told of a sower, of wheat among tares, of a harvest and a burning, He was not speaking a new tongue; He was speaking the oldest one.
A hearer who knew that flesh is grass, that the harvest is the day of the LORD, that the wicked are chaff and tares and the firstfruits are the LORD's own, needed no interpreter — the meaning was written already in the Law and the Prophets.
That is why He could say “Who hath ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 13:9), and why His astonishment that His own disciples could not decode the sower was just (Mark 4:13). [Footnote: That astonishment, and the exam it implies, is the argument of the chapter The Parables of the Kingdom.]

The words were sown centuries before; the parable only brought in the sheaves.
To read the New Testament by the Old is to reap what was long since planted.
